content: The document titled Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing was published in July 2021 as part of the World Health Organization's (WHO) efforts to provide evidence-based recommendations for expanding hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing services. The systematic review report, authored by Virginia A. Fonner and colleagues, evaluates the potential role of HCV self-testing (HCVST) as an additional approach to standard facility-based HCV testing services. The WHO guidelines on testing for hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HCV were last updated in February 2017. These guidelines emphasized the importance of facilityand community-based testing strategies to achieve WHO's elimination goals. Despite significant advancements in effective and affordable HCV treatments, many individuals with HCV remain unaware of their infection status due to limited access to and low uptake of testing services. Progress toward the 2030 targets of diagnosing 90% of HCV cases and treating 80% of those infected has been insufficient. Between 2015 and 2019, only 4 million people received treatment for HCV. Even in countries with robust national programs aimed at eliminating HCV as a public health threat, testing uptake has plateaued, and challenges persist in reaching key populations. Innovative approaches are urgently needed to identify undiagnosed individuals with HCV and link them to treatment. HCV self-testing is one such approach. Self-testing involves individuals collecting their own specimens, performing a simple rapid test, and interpreting their results. Those with reactive HCVST results require confirmatory testing to assess viremia and clinical evaluation before initiating treatment, following national diagnostic algorithms. Over the past five years, HIV self-testing (HIVST) has been successfully implemented in various settings and has proven effective in reaching populations that might not otherwise access HIV testing services. In 2016, WHO recommended HIVST as an additional approach to HIV testing services, and this recommendation was updated in 2019 based on evidence from 32 randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Building on the lessons learned from HIVST, small studies have explored the acceptability, usability, and feasibility of HCVST in priority settings and populations. However, WHO guidance on HCVST is needed to inform national policy decisions and implementation strategies. The systematic review aimed to address whether HCVST should be offered as an additional testing approach to complement existing HCV testing services. The review followed a structured PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) framework, focusing on populations receiving HCV testing services, the inclusion of self-testing in HCV testing services, and comparisons with standard facility-based testing services. Outcomes of interest were ranked by importance and priority, with critical outcomes including test uptake, positivity rates, linkage to care, and potential harms such as social harm or test misuse. The review included studies that compared HCVST to standard testing services, measured relevant outcomes, and were published in peer-reviewed journals or conference abstracts. Exclusion criteria included review articles, editorials, and opinion pieces without primary data. The search strategy was comprehensive, covering electronic databases, trial registries, and conference abstracts, and included input from experts in the field to identify unpublished or ongoing studies. The review also incorporated evidence from the HIVST literature, given its relevance to HCVST and the rigorous systematic review methods established for HIVST in the 2019 WHO guidelines. Comparable outcomes between HIVST and HCVST, such as test uptake, positivity, linkage to care, and harms, were analyzed. The review stratified outcomes by population type, including general and key populations at heightened risk for HCV, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), and individuals in high-prevalence settings. Data on values and preferences related to HCVST were identified through systematic reviews, community-based studies, and the HIVST evidence base. These data provided insights into the acceptability and feasibility of HCVST among different populations. Feasibility and resource needs for HCVST implementation were summarized, including findings from a commissioned cost-effectiveness study. Full reports on feasibility and resource needs are available as separate annexes. The review process was supported by an independent methodologist contracted by WHO, who provided guidance on the review methodology and ensured the rigor of the evidence synthesis. The findings of this systematic review aim to inform WHO's recommendations on HCVST and support countries in expanding their HCV testing and treatment programs to achieve elimination targets.
